tier_reason: The 13%/44% storage figures are in the arXiv:2201.01174 abstract (JEA 27, 2022), but that paper measures the authors' C++ code in FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp and never mentions xorf. xorf's own evidence is first-party: its docs say BinaryFuse8 uses about 9 bits per entry at about 2^-8 FP, and a doc test asserts fewer than 9.1 bits per entry. Its benches/ time only xorf's own filters and never a Bloom filter, so the Bloom side is theoretical and the evidence is C, not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README (qualitative): "Xor filters are faster and smaller than Bloom and Cuckoo filters." xorf's own docs (src/bfuse8.rs) say a BinaryFuse8 filter uses about 9 bits per entry at a false-positive rate of about 2^-8 (<0.4%), and a doc test asserts fewer than 9.1 bits per entry. The crate never measures a Bloom filter. The Bloom comparison exists only in the binary fuse paper (arXiv:2201.01174), measured on the authors' C++ implementation: binary fuse filters are within 13% of the storage lower bound versus 44% for Bloom filters.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 171 stars; crates.io `xorf` has about 6.7M total downloads (about 2.16M recent); latest crates.io version is 0.13.0
corrections.caveats: No Bloom or cuckoo filter is benchmarked anywhere in the crate: benches/ covers only xorf's own xor, fuse and binary fuse types. The 13%/44% figures come from the binary fuse paper, measured on FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp (C++, GCC 10 -O3 -march=native, i7-6700), and that paper does not mention this Rust port. The memory advantage follows from the algorithm's array sizing, and xorf's doc test (under 9.1 bits per entry) matches the paper's 9 bits per key, so it should carry over. It is still unmeasured against Bloom for this code. Query and build speed are not established for this implementation.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C. Table 2 of arXiv:2103.02515, by the author of RocksDB Ribbon, benchmarks Standard Ribbon w=128 against RocksDB's own FastLocalBloom and another blocked Bloom filter. The code is public in pdillinger/fastfilter_cpp (dev branch: benchmarks/bulk-insert-and-query.cc, driven by benchmarks/ribbon-benchmark.sh, with src/ribbon/ribbon_impl.h copied from RocksDB). The paper states an Intel Xeon D-2191 (Skylake DE) and GCC 8.4.1 with g++ -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=skylake-avx512. The blog's filter_bench numbers are verified verbatim but give no hardware.

corrections.claimed_speedup: arXiv:2103.02515 Table 2, at an FP rate around 1% (r=7): Standard Ribbon w=128 (the 128-bit variant RocksDB ships) has 6-8% space overhead over the information-theoretic bound, depending on n. RocksDB's FastLocalBloom blocked Bloom has 49.8% and another blocked Bloom has 52.0%. The cost is CPU: at n=10^6, Ribbon takes 166 vs 21 ns/key to build and 58 vs 10 ns/key to query; at n=10^8 it is 235 vs 72 and 140 vs 36 ns/key. The RocksDB blog (2021-12-29) gives ~30% space savings for 3-4x CPU (typical 7 bits/key Ribbon vs 10 bits/key Bloom at the same FP rate). It also says 100M keys in one filter still save 27% vs 30% at 100K keys. Its filter_bench figures are 140 vs 32 ns/key to construct (~4.4x, derived from page data) and 600 vs 500 ns/key to query (~20% slower, derived from page data).
corrections.workload: Static-filter space overhead, construction time and query time at an FP rate around 1% for n=10^6 and 10^8 keys. Source: the Ribbon paper's fastfilter_cpp fork benchmark (bulk-insert-and-query.cc via ribbon-benchmark.sh), which runs a copy of RocksDB's ribbon_*.h code against RocksDB FastLocalBloom and other Bloom variants. Also the RocksDB blog's filter_bench figures (`./filter_bench -impl=2|3 -quick -m_keys_total_max=200 -use_full_block_reader`, 'Random filter' queries).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 8.4.1, g++ -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=skylake-avx512 (paper Table 2); not stated for the blog's filter_bench numbers
corrections.hardware: Single-socket Intel Xeon D-2191 (Skylake DE), 64GB RAM (paper Table 2); not stated for the blog's filter_bench numbers
corrections.caveats: Tier A rests on arXiv:2103.02515. The paper has no journal reference on arXiv and no Crossref record, so the earlier claim that it 'appeared at ESA 2021' could not be verified and is dropped. The paper benchmarks a 2021 copy of RocksDB's ribbon_*.h code (Facebook copyright headers) inside the pdillinger/fastfilter_cpp fork (last pushed 2021-04-27). That is neither RocksDB's in-database filter path nor its current code. The memory win costs CPU: Ribbon construction is 3-8x slower and queries are several times slower than RocksDB's FastLocalBloom (Table 2), so RocksDB recommends a Ribbon+Bloom hybrid policy for long-lived levels. The blog's filter_bench numbers state no hardware or compiler.
